utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and to those listening to these procedures. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj. Welcome back. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye is carrying on his cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Kralj. When we left off yesterday --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't wait for the translation. When we left off yesterday I had shown you a document, 65 ter 5106, which I will leave at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender that document, and I would also like to let the Trial Chamber know --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And also you, Mr. Kralj --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that we have an original of the document, if either the Chamber would like to see it or review it, the Defence, or Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would ask you if you are going to show it to the witness so that he has a better look at it and to identify the handwriting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea, Mr. President. I will do that. And with the assistance of the usher, I will ask to have that placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I should also tell you that the ERN number that corresponds to the original is different than the one in e-court, and the reason is because the original document -- rather, the document in e-court was received as a photocopy prior to the original being received and so they were stamped separately but they are identical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, you are referring to page 12 in B/C/S and page 17 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be brought up in e-court. And page 12 in B/C/S should be put on the ELMO. Now we have it on the ELMO and you, Mr. Vanderpuye, should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, are you able to see the page that I referred you to yesterday in that original document? If it would be helpful for you to take it off the ELMO for a moment, have a good look at it, and then replace it, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no need. Having viewed these original documents, I can see that it is my handwriting, the word "no" in the Latin script. I was confused by the words in the Cyrillic script. Since we can see that the note says, "Kralj, why not?" that could have been General Tolimir's question. When I looked at the first page with approved convoys, I could see that even if Milovanovic had something to ask, he would have done it differently; in other words, I retract my previous statement now having viewed the originals. "Ne," or "no" is in the Latin script and this is what I usually use. It was my comment regarding this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could move the document so we can see the ERN number that would be helpful. Just on the record, the page that Mr. Kralj has been looking at is ERN 06793462, and once I get the document back I will provide the Trial Chamber with the range for that particular document so it's clear on the record. Thank you very much. I don't have any further use for that document, and I would tender the 65 ter 5106, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, and the original documents should be given back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5106 shall be assigned Exhibit P2858. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the ERN range of the document I've just shown Mr. Kralj is 06793451 through 06793463. I am not sure if the record reflects this, but I think it ought to, if not that Mr. Gajic I think had an opportunity to look at this document. I am not sure if Mr. Tolimir did as well, but at least the record should reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, when we left off yesterday aside from this document we were talking about 1995 and what was going on at that time in your sector with respect to the processing of convoy requests and related matters. Now, it was the case in 1995 that when General Milovanovic was present that General -- rather, Colonel Djurdjic could and would, on occasion, consult with General Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could engage in consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would be in relation to UNPROFOR convoys and humanitarian convoys; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more in relation to UNPROFOR convoys, because the general was a member of the joint military commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Prior to 1995, was it the case that Colonel Djurdjic would consult on the issues of convoys with General Tolimir? And I am talking about humanitarian convoys, anyway.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clarify, please. When prior to 1995? I only arrived there in late 1994, so I am not quite familiar with that topic, although there were humanitarian convoys. In the period before my arrival in the Main Staff, I don't know whether there were consultations with General Tolimir on the issue of humanitarian convoys. All documents which came to the 1st Corps were signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So when General Milovanovic wasn't around, was indeed in Crna Rijeka, Han Pijesak, wherever he might be to deal with these matters, did Colonel Djurdjic deal with humanitarian convoys or consult General Tolimir about the disposition of humanitarian convoys while you were there; that is, during the period of time that you were in that unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic, usually and for the most part, consulted with General Milovanovic. If either General Tolimir or someone else could be of assistance, he could turn to him to clarify certain things but not with respect to the quantities, size, and approval to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I would like to do is to -- I think I will show you this time 65 ter 7583.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I am going to ask if we could show, please, page 2956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I take it that you requested leave to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list yesterday, and I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if there is any objection to add this document to this list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there is again a problem with this microphone. Please stop. The interpreters can't hear you speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May peace reign in this house for all those present, and may God's will be done in these proceedings. I do not object to presenting anything that is necessary to Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Leave is granted to add it to the exhibit list. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I understand that we should be looking at page 30 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And starting at line 13, you can see the question here: "Who was the immediate superior of Colonel Djurdjic?" Your answer was: "His immediate superior was General Mladic, who later transferred part of the authorities from the sphere of humanitarian activities to the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic." And then you were asked this question: "What happened when the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, was not present at Crna Rijeka? In such cases, who would deal with humanitarian aid convoys and their movement?" And your answer was that: "In that situation, Colonel Djurdjic would consult on the issue of the convoys with General Tolimir." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I do want to add that I had UNPROFOR convoys in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see the question refers to humanitarian aid convoys and their movement. Are you saying that you may have misunderstood the question, Mr. Kralj? Let me just add this was put to you by Madam Natacha Fauveau who was the defence attorney for General Miletic. We can go to the previous page if you would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. Colonel Djurdjic, if he was unable to receive comments from General Milovanovic if there was no one there, the next person he could turn to in order to clarify things was General Tolimir irrespective of whether he was authorised to do that or not. By virtue of General Tolimir's position and his position in the various commissions, could consult with Colonel Djurdjic or, in turn, tell him to wait until General Milovanovic's return. He could share with him pieces of information that Colonel Djurdjic could use in his work. If authorised, he could also tell him, This is okay. Keep going, so as not to halt the entire convoy movement. It all depended on what authority he received from the commander and if he did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not sure exactly how to go about this. I don't intend to tender the entire transcript at this point, but I certainly would like to tender at least this page of it because it's germane to the issues in his -- in his cross-examination so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please put on the record the page number so that we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The page number is transcript page 29256. The specific -- the specific issue that arises from it is the question and answer found at lines 17 through 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This page will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 30 of the 65 ter document 7583 shall be assigned Exhibit P2859. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The humanitarian aid convoys at some point in 1995, I think it was March 1995, you testified on direct -- rather, the humanitarian aid -- co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid, rather, took over handling UNPROFOR convoys and movements at some point in 1995 in March; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be right. The co-ordinating body did not deal with UNPROFOR convoy movements. Perhaps this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to have it clear for the record. So UNPROFOR convoy movements were dealt with by the Main Staff throughout 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would entail the approvals and decision-making that we -- that you talked about earlier both on your direct and cross-examination; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add something, though. Colonel Djurdjic with an UNPROFOR representative, Colonel Coiffet, who was his peer, occasionally conducted analyses in order to address the problems relating to UNPROFOR convoy movements. They met at either Sokolac or in the UNPROFOR office at Pale. It was done in order to improve the co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for your answer. I -- I am not sure if you answered my question, though. My question was that the handling of UNPROFOR convoys and movements dealt with by the Main Staff throughout 1995, did that entail what you talked about before which was the process of approving it, regulating it, as it were, evaluating it? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I would kindly ask the Prosecution to upload page 29256 as a separate document because that was not in private session. This is not confidential. The whole transcript is under seal and this is the best way to avoid any conflict, and I was told that this relevant part of the testimony of Mr. Kralj in Popovic was not -- was in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The state co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid in 1995 dealt with the movement of humanitarian aid personnel, so to speak, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think you testified that Colonel Milos Djurdjic was the co-ordinator for the committee's relation with the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff of the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he acted on behalf of the Main Staff as the co-ordinating personal in charge of liaising with the co-ordinating body, but I don't think he was in charge of relations with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. He was a member of that co-ordinating body; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And a member of the Main Staff subordinated to General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And part of his function on that co-ordinating body was to represent the interests of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So he expressed concerns that the VRS had with respect to the movement of humanitarian aid convoys as well as with respect to the quality and quantity of the goods or items they requested to move?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was more in terms of control and convoy movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that he did not express concerns that the VRS had with respect to the movement of humanitarian aid, or are you saying that he did that in addition to dealing with matters of control and convoy movements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could acquaint the co-ordination body with some kinds of goods that can be used for military purposes but are carried by humanitarian convoys, by Muslim soldiers, or he could give information that he was -- that was at his disposal to the effect that these goods were not to be used for the civilian population but rather for supplying the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One of his functions was to transmit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One of his functions was to transmit the decision of the co-ordinating body to the Main Staff - isn't that right? - or communicating?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The co-ordinating body reported to the Main Staff in writing. He could only submit his own written report about where he was and what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And after the co-ordinating body, you said that they reported to the Main Staff, what do you mean by that? You mean that they reported their decisions or determinations to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The co-ordinating body did not file reports with the Main Staff. The colonel submitted reports about his work to the Main Staff; whereas, the co-ordinating body, if it took any decisions, informed the Main Staff of the procedures the Main Staff is to abide by in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a translation issue, but at page 11, line 1 - and I know that you can read English - you are recorded in the transcript as saying that "the co-ordinating body reported to the Main Staff in writing." That's the reason why I asked the question. But let me ask this question: The decisions that were made by the co-ordinating body, those -- the Main Staff was informed of these - is that right? - in writing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And once that decision was issued, it was up to the Main Staff to make sure that the subject of the humanitarian aid convoy decision was abided by?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so the Main Staff communicated the decision of the co-ordinating body to subordinate units and organs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that was so that the passage of these convoys, their movement, the movement of personnel, and the cargo could be properly regulated, inspected, and controlled; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There would have been no further need to communicate the Main Staff's particular take on a decision by the co-ordinating body once it had issued a decision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The co-ordinating body dealt with all its activities through the Main Staff, activities that had to do with the movement of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I can show you 65 ter 3282 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I can have that on the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this document is already Exhibit P1692. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am reminded by Ms. Stewart that I -- I think I have read the number incorrectly. It should be 3238. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document is a little dark and it may be difficult for you to read, and perhaps if you can't read it you can read the English version, but if we could just focus in first on the top, we can see that this is from the Main Staff. The report number is 06/20-104, and it's dated 10 March 1995. And it's directed to the command of the Drina Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the East Bosnia Corps. And it says: "Please be advised that we approved the weekly plan of distribution of humanitarian assistance from Belgrade for eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period from 11 March until 17 March 1995." Before I move on, let me just ask this question: This is notified to the respective corps because that is the route that the convoy would be expected to take; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in order for a convoy to pass through these various corps, that needs to be co-ordinated or authorised by the Main Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then the second part -- rather, the very beginning of the first paragraph. It says: "Please be advised that we approved the weekly plan of the distribution of humanitarian assistance ..." Now, the weekly plan for the distribution of humanitarian assistance is something that's decided by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a mistake, an administrative error. Before the setting up of the co-ordination body, the term used was "we approve" so that it probably still lingered even after this co-ordination body had been set up. Old habits die hard. If something is approved, although not approved by the Main Staff, it has a certain weight for those manning the check-points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please rephrase his answer. The interpreter cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The co-ordination body's duty is to approve this part referring to the cargo carried. And the Main Staff, before this term "approval" began to be used, the Main Staff would give its consent to the co-ordination body with regard to the route. So the way it's phrased here is wrong. This is actually approved by the co-ordination body. In some other reports we saw that the co-ordination body did issue approvals. Those who were more careful drafting these documents put it right; whereas here by inertia the former -- the formerly used expressions are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There was some part of your answer that I understand there was some difficulty interpreting. It was a rather lengthy answer, and I am not sure exactly where it arises. Perhaps we can find that. Let's see if we can clarify this for you. Where you said: "If something is approved, although not approved by the Main Staff, it has a certain weight for those manning the check-points." From that point, until the point where you said: "The co-ordination body's duty is to approve this part referring to the cargo carried." In between those two phrases, the interpreter was not able to follow what you were saying. Can you recall what you were saying after you said that: "If something is approved, although not approved by the Main Staff, it has a certain weight for those manning the check-points." Do you remember what you said after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but let me simplify this. For a while the Main Staff approved humanitarian convoys. After the setting up of the co-ordinating body, the Main Staff no longer had this duty. It was -- that was no longer part of its remit. Everybody was advised to submit their requests through the co-ordinating body. And during a transitional period, because it took some time for everybody to understand that it was the co-ordinating body that was in charge of convoys, there could be such mistakes as here where it says "we approved." It was up to the co-ordinating body to approve these things. This is merely wrongly phrased. I hope this was clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Thank you very much. Following the -- well, rather, the second sentence of this paragraph says: "We reduced the plan for enclaves in number of vehicles and the transport of fuel is not permitted." My question is: If the co-ordinating body had approved the plan, what does this reduction refer to -- or, rather, why is the plan being reduced?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about goods such as fuel or something else from which there was intelligence that reserves are being formed or that they were being used by the army in the enclaves. There could be restrictions with regard to them imposed by the Main Staff because there was a state of war, after all, and things like this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you down to the remark. It's at the -- near the bottom of the page. And it says: "Regarding medicine for Srebrenica, approved for 14 March 1995, we shall send to the command of the Drina Corps a separate list of medicine once we co-ordinate it."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This remark may have meant the list of medication has not been checked by our medical service to establish its possible purpose. Colonel Djurdjic often forwarded such lists to the medical services of the Main Staff for them to check what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kralj. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to tender, Mr. President, this document, 65 ter 3238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2860. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic. We would request the Registry to ask the technicians during one break to do something with the microphone of Mr. Gajic and the microphone of Mr. Tolimir. Both have some problems with that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, about this document, I would like it to be marked for identification until the final version of the translation. I think that the last sentence of paragraph one is not correctly translated. In the Serbian version, it says, "plan smo sacinili." [In English] "We put together." [Interpretation] "We made or drafted plan," whereas the translation reads, "We put together a plan." That may give rise to a confusion in people reading this translation, this very last sentence of paragraph one, which in the translation reads: "We put together a plan based on authorisation from the co-ordinating body ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Gajic, that this is more a request for clarification and for checking the correct translation of the document. The document will remain as an exhibit, but this request we take it and we will deal with that, and I think this resolves the problem. This is the normal procedure if there are any doubt if the translation is correct. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Of course this is the regular procedure. I would just like to direct your attention to the initial phrase in that sentence which reads, "We put together ..." I believe that this may not be fully clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now on the record and the relevant people will deal with that. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have a concern that I'd like to express to the Trial Chamber, but I don't think I can do it in the presence of the witness. I would just ask if he could just be excused for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. Mr. Kralj, you've heard the request of Mr. Prosecutor. Please leave the courtroom for a moment and you will be called back soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My concern is - and it's really not that big a deal - but my concern is in respect of Mr. Gajic's objection to the admission of the document or the translation issues that concern it. With this particular witness, he does speak English, he's fluent in English, as I think he testified, and obviously in his own language. My concern is that when those types of objections are made in front of the witness, it might signal to him, obviously, to question either the document or the translation of the document and that kind of thing. So I don't mind that Mr. Gajic makes an objection, I think it's appropriate for him to do that, but if it's of the nature, he can simply say, I have an objection to the quality of this particular translation. But to flag specific provisions in front of the witness I think is more problematic. But I don't -- as I said, it's not a big deal, but just in the future, during the course of the cross-examination, I think it might be better to deal with it in a more obtuse way, in a broader way, rather than so specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you get the floor, Mr. Gajic. I would like to clarify. It was not an objection to the admission of this document. It was a question if the translation is correct, and we should recall the rules in this courtroom and this trial is not for Mr. Gajic to address the Chamber with objections. That would be the task of Mr. Tolimir himself as an accused who is representing himself. Mr. Gajic has a limited role to play in this courtroom. But I understand your concern, and I think such a request to check if the translation is correct may be addressed to the Chamber in the absence of a witness, not to influence him. On the other hand, Mr. Tolimir has the right to check these matters with the witness during his re-examination. So I think in that way we can resolve this problem. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I deliberately waited until the witness finished his answer before I made my comment. I only pointed out one term that can be differently understood. It was not part of the examination of the Prosecutor. I was -- I only pointed out a phrase that was a bit vaguely translated. I am not saying that it does not correspond to the original but it may give rise to the confusion. But this matter will not be raised in re-examination because the witness has already answered what the procedure was to approve the movement of humanitarian convoys so that it would be only the repetition of something already dealt with. I think that with regard to this specific question, I think that the timing was right because the answer had already been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am content to leave it like this, and with the Court's leave, I would like to have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. I think in that way we have no conflict anymore. We agreed that these matters should not be dealt with during the examination of a specific document but only after that, and we leave it like this. The witness should be brought in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Kralj. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, I would like to show you another document. It's 65 ter 5729. And I think you can see here that this is a document from the Main Staff. It is report number 06/20-111 and it is directed to the Drina Corps command. And in this document it says: "We hereby inform you that we agree to the implementation of the UNHCR Belgrade weekly plan for which approval number 0468-HCR-288 was given." And then it proceeds to discuss how the plan is to be implemented. And my question to you is: Here you can see that the term "we agreed" to the implementation of the plan is used. Is that due to the same reasons that you gave with respect to the other document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the bottom of this document - and we'll to go to page 2 in the English - we see a note. And under that note it says: "In addition to the quantities of beef given for Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa, which have been reduced fourfold, the transport" -- "the transport," rather, "of the following has not been approved ..." And then there is a list of things: Oxygen bottles, matches, plywood panels for Srebrenica; matches and motor oil for Zepa; and oxygen bottles for Gorazde. If the plan was approved - in this case we can see that the quantities of beef have been reduced fourfold - is that due to the same reasons that you gave with respect to the other document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was due to the same reasons, but I wanted to add that individual humanitarian organisations absent this note, which had previously been agreed upon with the co-ordinating body, tried to submit the original plan at the check-points so as to be allowed to transport quantities which were not allowed. That is why this note was put in to pay attention to the quantities because sometimes they would show another plan which they had submitted original simply trying to have it processed the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When they submitted a plan, that is the humanitarian aid agencies, with respect to the passage of a convoy, they would have to show one that was approved, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if they submitted a plan that was the original plan, it would have had to have been approved in order for them to even think about showing it at a check-point; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 75 -- I'm sorry, 5728 -- yeah, one more correction. 5729 shall be assigned Exhibit P2861. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show you P2507. This is another document concerning -- well, rather, it's another document from the Main Staff. It's dated 22 April, 1995, report number 06/17-368. And this one says -- it's directed to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. So it deals with UNPROFOR movements. And it says: "We hereby inform you that we have not approved the movement of the following convoys," and it lists them. It's one through eleven. And it is signed by General Milovanovic. I would like to go through this document just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the first page -- I'm sorry, the second page in the B/C/S, and the third page in the English. Yeah, I think we have got that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to do is focus on the handwriting at the very top of the page. Do you recognise the handwriting at the top of the page and the initial or signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And whose signature or initials is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: ZT, Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the handwriting as well, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Fair to say it's the same person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can zoom out just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This particular convoy refers to the passage of a convoy number 23-309/04 [Realtime transcript read in error "23-2309/04"] through the check-point on Kobiljaca. It refers to one of the purposes being to provide fuel. You can see that in a kind of a square -- a rectangle, rather, that's marked in pen. And it's for all units in the Sarajevo sector. This particular convoy was not approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Put the convoy number on the record again, please, because it was incorrectly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The convoy number was 23-309/04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just for the record, it's listed as convoy number 1 on the first page of this document. If we could just go to the next page in both -- page 5 in English, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we can see another convoy. Same signature -- or, rather, same initials, same handwriting; right, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this convoy request concerns the movement of a company of the Main Staff of the BH command from Sarajevo to Kiseljak of UNPROFOR, obviously. It in part requests fuel, you can see it says "diesel," that's underlined, and then 30 cubic metres of diesel with respect to a Sarajevo-bound convoy at item number 6. That's on page 6 of the English translation. If we go to item number 2, it says that: "The purpose of the journey is to provide the company of the Main Staff of the BH Command of UNPROFOR with diesel for vehicles and generators of the company of the Main Staff." Was it your understanding that there was a prohibition on the fuel made available to the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no restrictions, but there were attempts to supply the UNPROFOR command with excessive quantities of oil or fuel, which would then be put on some convoys in an attempt for it to reach the enclaves. That is why the restrictions were imposed. Of course, the UNPROFOR command had to specify a request in order to receive additional quantities of fuel. This is what the Main Staff noticed and that is why the restrictions were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I would like to do is to take you to page number 10 in the B/C/S, and I believe it's 19 in the English. Yes, that's right. At the top of this page we can see, again, the initials. Are they the same, first of all, that you identified previously?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials are the same but I think the handwritten note reads: "Linked to the next request." Well, it could all be the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can zoom out, please, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This convoy request is 23-02 and corresponds to item number 9 on the first page of this document. And it concerns a request for the movement from Zepa to Sarajevo of a convoy and it relates to the movement of certain personnel. And it says: "Purpose of journey: Transfer from Zepa." That's underlined. And the personnel concerned are UN military observers. Do you see that under item number 4? Are you able to make that out, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This convoy also was not approved. And if you can look -- maybe we need to go to the next page in the English. We have this personnel, and they have described that they would be using a Land Cruiser with a UN license plate number 9818, and it lists the following cargo: Personal equipment: Five binoculars, two Sony walkman, a Toshiba walkman, one Sony radio, one Philips radio, three bullet-proof jackets and helmets, one compass, one capset which has to be taken to be repaired. Let me show you the next one which will be page 21 in the English. Yes, and we have it in the B/C/S as well. This is convoy number 23-03, and it's related, obviously, to the one that precedes it. This one says, "ne," and it has these same initials. Same person; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials are definitely the same, and I suppose it is the same person. Can I comment something, though?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This illustrates frequent movements of military observers with a single vehicle from the enclaves to Sarajevo. What else was for the military observers to do than to observe the situation in the field and forward reports to their superior command? That was the only reason why. Sometimes in critical security situations some restrictions were imposed on their passage. Colonel Djurdjic monitored exactly how many times each military observer went one way or the other. The conclusion was that they were observing our communications more than observing the area they were mandated to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, the link between these two documents is an interesting one because the convoy 23-02 relates to personnel that are leaving the area of Zepa, and this one relates to personnel going in. In effect, what you see here is a rotation; right, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if this request is denied, it means that these units cannot rotate; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, this could perhaps have been in a specific period and no rotations could take place then. What followed was subsequent discussions between Djurdjic and Coiffet or their military representative where such issues were being discussed and decisions made as to when specific rotations could take place. It didn't mean that there were no rotations at all. It just meant that they probably took place later on when people from the Main Staff and the UNPROFOR command who were in charge of relaying such information agreed. I think on our side there was Colonel Milos, I believe that was his name, and Colonel Coiffet on behalf of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, in this particular document you can see these troops -- or, rather, observers, are being proposed to rotate in for the ones that were coming out in request 23-02. But they are also rotating -- requested to rotate in with certain supplies. The other request that is to take observers out of Zepa, you will remember, listed a capset which was in need of repair. And here under item 5 you can see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we will have to go to page 22 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see that the capset or a capset is being proposed to replace the broken one in Zepa. In addition to that, the request is for personnel equipment, a couple of shovels, a radio receiver with headphones, a couple of spare wheels, a battery charger and some batteries, a walkman, Sony radio, an adapter, a couple of speakers, a videotape, a radio with headphones, one carton of juice, 6 litres of orange juice, a couple of kilogrammes of chicken, some cigarettes, some sweets and vegetables, presumably for the units that are still there in Zepa. Can you see any real obvious military reason to restrict this rotation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly why this was not approved, but I'll try to clarify. The equipment that was used and that was specified on this list was not for the needs of the unit but for the needs of the specific three observers if let through so that they would have it for their consumption or a certain period of time, or perhaps to give it to someone else since there was a general shortage of milk, sugar, and coffee, so that they could play host to someone else in the enclave with whom they were in contact. Military observers were usually accommodated separately from the UNPROFOR seat or office in the enclaves. They had a different house or facilities. This is for their use, not for others. If the entire document was not approved, it means that none of it was let through, at least not at that time. Perhaps it was approved later unless there were certain restriction, if it was deemed that they carried equipment that was not necessary. It was part of the regular conversations between Colonel Djurdjic and Colonel Coiffet. I know that there were specific issues with arranging such rotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the general problem and that they met frequently. Apparently there were too many requests for rotations and observer movement. The observers rotated more frequently than was customary. That is what I was talking about. What does it mean? Under the excuse of rotation, they actually carried out reconnaissance along the routes they moved. They could, for example, go once from our territory to the other and then observe the situation on their way back as well. If they did the same trip five times, they reconnoitred five times. If it happens within only 15 days, then their activity was controlled. That is why such rotations were often in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kralj, you probably know this, having testified for the Miletic Defence and now for the Tolimir Defence, but it is the Prosecution's case in this case - as it was in the Popovic case - that these kinds of restrictions and limitations on UNPROFOR's activities and their ability to rotate and their ability to supply their forces was a deliberate act that was engaged in by the VRS in collusion with the RS authorities to strangle those enclaves and to effect a policy that had been put in place at least since March of 1995. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not busy myself with politics. I dealt with specific issues, and my knowledge refers to the implementation of convoy passage as well as to movement along specific routes in and out of the enclave. Politics took place on a higher level and I was not privy to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document -- oh, I'm sorry. It's in. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am prepared to move to my next topic after the break, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We need now our first break and we will resume at 12.00 -- at 11.00. Sorry, at 11.00, the usual half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, we were talking about a convoy request with respect to some UN military observers going in and out of Zepa, and I'd asked you a question about your knowledge concerning policies that were in place with respect to restricting their ability to rotate. This Trial Chamber has received evidence, and in particular I am referring to the testimony of a UN military observer, who stated as follows. At page 5644 of the transcript of this trial, the question was put to him by the Honourable Judge Nyambe: "I have just one question for you, Mr. Kingori: How many UN observers were involved towards the fall of Srebrenica and during the fall of Srebrenica?" The answer was: "Your Honour, initially we were six military observers in Srebrenica, but three of them were unable to get -- were allowed to get out of the enclave during the normal rotation. We used to get -- after you work continuously for that days, you're allowed to go out of the enclaves after six days, but this time the three had been denied permission by the BSA to go out until it reached a point whereby the three of them were to go out at the same time. So they were allowed at that time, but no replacement was allowed for these three. So we remained, the three of us, in the enclave." And his answer continues. He also provided evidence in the Popovic case, the one in which you testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is for the benefit of our Trial Chamber, Exhibit P950. If we have it in e-court, then it will be page 20 in e-court, otherwise I will just identify for the record what I am reading from. It's at page -- transcript page 19171 through 172, starting at line 20. The question was: "Now, sir --" 19171 we will need in the -- that's just the previous page, I think, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question is put at line 18: "Now, sir, in June 1995, did anything happen that affected the size of your team?" This is the same observer. Answer: "Your Honour, this is the time that some of the UNMOs who were inside the enclave finished their time of staying. In fact, if we start slightly before that, we had every month, after working 30 days, a" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "... an UNMO would be given six days off so that he can go back to Zagreb, or whatever he wants, so that he can relax and come back already refreshed so that he can be used better. "During that period," this is at ending page 172, "that is, somewhere in [sic] April, they started denying that UNMOS, that is, the BSA started denying the UNMOs permission to leave the enclave. So there was a long stay until three observers were due now for rotation, and the BSA said they cannot give clearance for them to get out. So, later on, they allowed them to get out; and upon their exit they said they cannot allow anybody else to come in to replace them. "So, in effect, we were left, just three of us; me, myself; Major Andre De Haan from Holland; and Major David Tetteh from Ghana. Those were the only observers who were left in the enclaves at that time." Now, having read that to you, Mr. Kralj, let me ask you first: Are you aware of these restrictions as concerns the UNMOs, UN military observers, related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not privy to these matters relating to military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about matters relating to the rotation of DutchBat troops in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am only familiar with that document I recognised, and I know that there were talks between Milos and UNPROFOR representatives about rotation. I was not personally involved in rotation-related matters, nor did I know how many military observers there were in Srebrenica, who they were, nor did I ever have a chance to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also received evidence from a DutchBat officer regarding this or a similar issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's P598. If we have it, it should be e-court page 18. And for the record, it's transcript page number 2449 from the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The same one in which you testified. And the question is at line 15. Question: "Now, how about with respect to the DutchBat troop rotations, sir? Were there restrictions placed on DutchBat's ability to rotate its soldiers in and out?" Answer: "Yeah, well, we could say till the end of March or April that was -- there were problems with those convoys, personnel convoys, but that was more teasing than operational danger, in fact, but as of April it was finished. We had quite a lot of guys out who couldn't come in anymore." He's asked about what the fighting strength of his unit was, and he answers beginning at line 25: "About 300. To be exact, I believe 318." At page 2450, question: "And after the VRS restrictions kicked in, sir, you mentioned that you had a lot of soldiers who couldn't come in anymore. What were you down to? "A. In the end we had 147. Question: "And during this time when you were experiencing these restrictions, did you have a team [sic] that you used within the battalion for what was going on? "A. Yes. We called that convoy terror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think you misspoke in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "A term." You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "A term" instead of "a team."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Kralj, is: These DutchBat soldiers rotated in and out or were to rotate in and out by way of a convoy, a personnel convoy. That's something that would be directed to your sector, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All requests for UNPROFOR passage should have been notified in line with the regular procedure through my sector. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so the denial of convoy requests to move personnel by UNPROFOR is something that would be handled by your sector and the personnel within the Main Staff that you indicate -- indicated previously dealt with those matters, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector dealt with the administrative matters and with the implementation of procedures that were required for the movement of UNPROFOR convoys in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you a Defence exhibit in this case, D122.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will have to go to page -- it should be 93 in the B/C/S. And in the English it should be page 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This, as you can see, is a report from the Secretary-General pursuant to the General Assembly Resolution 53/35 regarding the fall of Srebrenica. What it talks about in this particular -- well, if you begin at paragraph 233 it talks about the squeeze of the enclave by the BSA, as it's referred to here, or the VRS. And it says at paragraph 233: "The BSA continued to tighten their squeeze on the safe area from mid-February onward, progressively limiting the already restricted flow of humanitarian aid into the enclave and constraining the provision of supplies to DutchBat." I would like to take you to paragraph 235 which we will find at page 94 in the B/C/S, same page I think in the English. And here it talks about the commanding officer of DutchBat, who says -- in the second sentence it says: "He complained that since 26 April the BSA had not allowed a single member of his battalion to leave the enclave or enter it (thus, those who had gone on leave previously were unable to return, lowering the battalion's strength by approximately 150 soldiers)." You saw just a moment ago in the testimony of a DutchBat officer. It says: "He added that there had been no food delivered in March. No fresh food, dairy products, flour products or meat had been brought into the enclave since May." And that: "The BSA had also continued their now four-month-old restrictions on spare parts and engineering equipment being brought in for the battalion." And that: "They also blocked supplies of fuel for UNPROFOR which resorted to borrowing fuel from the UNHCR and to replacing vehicle patrols with foot patrols." My question is pretty much the same, Mr. Kralj. The effects that the commanding officer of DutchBat is talking about are directly related to the approval or disapproval of convoy requests which would have passed through your sector; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. No decisions as to letting something pass or not were taken in our sector. Only the commander was in a position to make such decisions:

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Your sector processed those request, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Administratively.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P710. This you can -- this document, you can see, is a cable. It's directed to Kofi Annan. It's dated 18 April 1995. It's a UN document. And it refers to air resupply to the eastern enclaves and Sarajevo. And under item number 2, it says: "All of the air planning is in response to previous and current BSA intransigence in refusing requests for fuel and other convoys into Sarajevo and the enclaves. Should this situation worsen and should the BSA wish to use resupply as a political and military lever, then the contingency plan must exist for using helicopters for resupply of UN forces." If we go on to item number 4 which should be on it next page for both documents, it says: "The following additional information further clarifies the situation." Under item A, it says: "Srebrenica." And it says that: "Srebrenica has been using UNHCR stocks of diesel fuel of which 38.4 cubic metres have been used so far. The battalion reduced consumption rates some three weeks -- some weeks ago to 3.5 cubic metres per day and has now cut consumption to 1.5 cubic metres per day. Strict limitations have been placed on the use of vehicles and generators. The operational effects have resulted in a much reduced patrolling programme." That's for Srebrenica. For Zepa, which is item number C, it says that: "No vehicle -- there is no vehicle patrolling in Zepa and the company is using wood for cooking and candles for light." This is in April of 1995. Those items would be, similarly, the subject of convoy requests handled administratively by your unit and approved or disproved by the commander of the Main Staff or whoever it is that the commander designates; isn't that right, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information you have put forward just now aren't anything I am familiar with, but you know that the sector dealt with the convoy passage from the administrative aspect. We were also involved in talks at the lower level with UNPROFOR about problems related to the passage of these convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, you said, "... about problems related to the passage of these convoys." What do you mean by that? What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I merely want to say that UNPROFOR did have contacts with Colonel Milos Djurdjic. They had an officer at the same level as Colonel Djurdjic and they dealt with problems with the passage of convoys. It may have been about the approval or non-approval of the passage. These problems would be discussed at meetings. They would call themselves and that occasionally took place either at the Pale office or at the Sokolac office. They had the opportunity to discuss in detail approvals or non-approvals from a previous period. The procedure didn't stop with the failure to approve a convoy. UNPROFOR could call a meeting and discuss the matter to see what the problem was, and there were such meetings, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I take from your answer that you were familiar with the problems occurring during these passages, especially problems because of a non-approval of the convoys; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am saying that Colonel Djurdjic was familiar with all information and all problems. I was an interpreter, and I knew what he was willing to tell me or what he considered as necessary for me to know to be able to draft a document related to convoys, which document was necessary for the work and the functioning of the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put this question to you because you said, "We were also involved in talks at a lower level with UNPROFOR," "we."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only had the opportunity once to be involved with Colonel Djurdjic in talks about the co-operation between UNPROFOR and our sector. I was there in the capacity of an interpreter. That's why I said "we," otherwise Colonel Djurdjic was the only one to attend such meetings. He relied on the interpreters from Pale who were very good. They were Serbs who were staying at Pale; whereas, the UNPROFOR officers were subordinate to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo, or to Colonel Coiffet who sent [indiscernible] notifications through them, and also through them received approvals or non-approvals. I was not part of the process. I was only able to stand in for Colonel Djurdjic in case of his absence but merely administratively. That means that Colonel Djurdjic was in charge of all matters related to the enclaves. I didn't even know how many soldiers there were in Srebrenica, and I can also add that I never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can go to the next page in the English. And I think there is a translation as well, at least of the headings, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what this reflects is an attachment referred to in item 5 of this document concerning the provisions that were made available to the enclaves, and it's a chart of UNHCR supplies. What I'd like to refer you to is the particular entries for Srebrenica and Zepa. You can see in the first column - January through April, that is - it says "requirements total." And for Srebrenica and Zepa it is 678 tonnes and 159 tonnes respectively. Then it says "requirements food." And you will see those numbers are the same. And then it says in the last column, January through April, "delivered." And I want to focus you particularly on the months of March and April. For Srebrenica in the month of March 1995, this reflects that 547 tonnes were delivered out of the 678 required. For the month of April that figure dropped to 363 of the 678 required. And for Zepa those figures were 124 tonnes of 159 for the month of March that made it through, and 68 out of 160 for the month of April. Were you aware that the amount of aid, in this case food being delivered to those enclaves, was dropping for those months as is indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, and I was not in charge of following the issue of what and how much entered the enclaves. I was not following the figures, whether they went up or down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you a Defence exhibit in this case. It's D209. This is an exhibit that General Tolimir showed you during the course of your direct examination. And it comes from someone by the name of Novakovic. Do you remember this document, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this document as something that was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I have to confess that I haven't gone through and done all the math on this document, but if we focus on the month of April for Zepa, you will see that the tonnage of material that month starts out with 77 tonnes, and that's of flour; 7 and a half tonnes of beans; 5 tonnes of beef; 7 tonnes -- it looks like oil, cooking oil. And the next tonnage entry looks like 2 tonnes of detergent and 0.4 tonnes of sanitary towels, I think. The total amount that was indicated in the document that I showed you before was about 68 tonnes out of 160 that were required. This one probably reflects - as I said I haven't done the math - a little bit more than 90 or between 90 and 100 out of 160. This is information that was given to you or provided, rather, to your sector; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was forwarded to the sector on request, but I wasn't in charge of this issue. I merely recognised the document and I know who sent it. As for the quantities, that is something I am seeing only for the second time. I saw it for the first time when General Tolimir showed it. This is the second time. I know, though, that the sector and Colonel Djurdjic received information, and I know who he received it from as well as who he sent information to as part of his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the month of April for Srebrenica, in this same document, you can see the tonnage reflects 387 tonnes of flour; 44 tonnes of beans; 21.6 tonnes of canned beef; and so on and so forth. You can see this all the way down the document. What I showed you just a moment ago, the UN report indicated that for the month of April in Srebrenica about 363 tonnes of goods got into the enclave. This document by Novakovic reflects what appears to be somewhere around 400 to 450 tonnes of the 678 that's indicated that would be required, which I submit to you is substantially less than what was required for that enclave. This is information that Colonel Djurdjic was made aware of; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen the plan put together by the international organisations or the co-ordinating body as to how much of what was planned to be forwarded to the enclaves. Perhaps it was at the level of the co-ordinating body, but I didn't see that document in the sector offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kralj, I am done with this document. Let me ask you a couple of other things. Let me show you P714. This as you can see is a document. It's a daily reporting to the Security Council. It's a UN document from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. Under item number 2 it reports that: "None of the UNHCR convoys to the enclaves have received clearances." By the way, this is the week -- I'm sorry, the date is 14 June 1995. "None of the UNHCR convoys to the enclaves have received clearances. The Srebrenica convoy has been cancelled. The Sarajevo convoy has not left Zenica." And it says: "The BSA are demanding a 50-50 share of the aid to which UNHCR will not agree. The UNPF resupply convoys have suffered a similar fate." Do you know about the restriction of these convoys as late as June 1995? Because before you referred to a period, and I was showing you a document in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear for the first time that this 50-50 share was something that was requested. I am not familiar with that. And I have no information about any restrictions in this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 7586.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. President, that I will need to add to the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since I have seen the document, I have no objection to having admitted documents which will only assist you in making the right decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have to say we don't have a B/C/S translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I will read parts of it, if that will assist you, Mr. Kralj. But I do know you speak English as well, so let me know if you need me to do that. But it is a weekly situation report. You can see at the top it says, "UNPROFOR Office of Civil Affairs." And then it has a number. The number is 108. And it says 26 February to 4 March 1995. What I would like to do is to take you to page 5 of this document, under item number 15, which talks about Srebrenica supplies. And it says here that: "After the UNPROFOR troops in Srebrenica literally ran out of food (they consumed their last combat rations on 03 March), the BSA finally agreed today after several prior refusals to allow the troops resupply. The BSA, explained that they have no objection to food deliveries, only to fuel, continue to refuse the delivery of fuel to Srebrenica and they continue to refuse medical supplies into the three eastern enclaves." Now, during this period of time this is -- I'm sorry, this is February through March, you would have been receiving requests for medical supplies, supplies for UNPROFOR troops in your department or sector? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a specific request, perhaps show it. There were some such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the situation with respect to the restriction of supplies to UNPROFOR and medical supplies in and around this period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I was not aware of a policy to impose restrictions on the goods specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But my question is: Were you aware of the situation that was developing as a result of the restrictions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have said already that I was not familiar with - and it was not part of my job as interpreter - to know what the situation was like and what the problems were in the protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Mr. Kralj, but my question isn't -- my question is, rather, did you know about it? Whether you were an interpreter or private citizen or in any other capacity.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew what I could learn from the media, but I had no specific knowledge. I was only aware of what was available to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7586 shall be assigned Exhibit P2862, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness P2091.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another UN document. I think we have a translation for this one. We do. It's dated 7 March 1995, and it is from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter to the commander. And it concerns a meeting between General Smith and General Mladic on 7 March 1995. You will see in the very first paragraph of this document your name, and in particular it says that a meeting took place between General Smith and General Mladic at a hotel. It says that the meeting was at the invitation of General Mladic and that General Smith joined the meeting directly from his visit to Srebrenica. It says that General Mladic was accompanied by Major-General Zivanovic, who was the commander of the Drina Corps at that time, and Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj, who he characterises here as an intelligence officer and interpreter on General Mladic's staff. Do you remember this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the meeting, but I have a correction to make. This is a mistake. I have never been an intelligence officer, only an interpreter --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, Mr. Kralj. Let me take you to item number 4 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will have to go to page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 4 in the English there is a heading, topical heading: "Humanitarian issues - enclaves." And it says: "Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error "Million"] asked General Smith for his impressions from his visit to Srebrenica. General Smith registered his concern over the shortages of medical supplies held by NGOs in the area and the general supply of shortages of DutchBat within the enclave." General Mladic reported that he had cleared food and medicine convoys to Srebrenica and Zepa over the last 24 hours. Do you remember this information being passed on to General Mladic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was an interpreter at this meeting. That was my capacity there. And I was far more busy with interpreting everything correctly than I paid attention to the contents. General Smith spoke the kind of English which posed problems to me. In other words, I do recall the meeting but I no longer remember the details. Only a document could jog my memory, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I was hoping this one would, but if it doesn't, I'll leave that be. Let me show you another document. It's another Defence document. It's D79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, on page 45, line 18, the first word should read "Mladic." Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, do you remember being shown this document during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerns a convoy from Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you item number 8, which should be on page 2 of both of these versions. It says under item number 8 - and this is in order - president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and this was directed to the Main Staff: "To allow departure of the teams of MSF (Medecins Sans Frontieres) from Gorazde and Srebrenica and postpone the entrance of new ones for an indefinite period of time." Were you aware of this particular document and this particular order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is something that Colonel Djurdjic would have been aware of; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ought to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's something that the generals in the Main Staff would have been aware of, too? An order from the president?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A presidential order is usually addressed to the commander of the Main Staff who then made decisions as to who should or should not be acquainted with the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular document, and item 8 specifically, the movement of teams of MSF workers is something that would fall within the purview of a humanitarian aid convoy or movement; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see at the bottom that it was sent to the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. It had to do with the work of that committee, first and foremost, because it was the committee who approved the passage of humanitarian organisations. As for the medical part, this was within the purview of a representative of the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let's go to page 1 of this document. The document as you can see is dated 13 June 1995; right? And it says: "On the basis of the conclusions of the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations made on 8 June 1995, I issue the following order:" Now, the movement of MSF workers or MSF supplies is something that should go through the co-ordinating committee as you've previously testified; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the regulation of the movement of those individuals or those supplies is something that is notified to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the Main Staff then notifies subordinate units or organs in order to inspect, control, and administer the passage of those people or goods; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So this is something that would have had to have gone to the Main Staff so that the Main Staff could do its job; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can always see from a document who it was addressed to. It either has the list of addressees at the bottom on the left-hand side or there is a stamp, a stamp confirming its receipt and registering.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So your answer is you don't know if the Main Staff received the document, I guess?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I have not seen it.
